name: Elena Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Elena, and thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate an electric rope shovel at an iron ore mine, which is a digger the size of a house that loads the haul trucks, about sixty tonnes a bucket. I lead the shovel crew on my roster, three shovels and their operators. My day is twelve hours: walk-around at the start, check the cables and the teeth on the bucket, then dig and load, dig and load, keeping four trucks happy. I love the rhythm of it when it's going well, and I love that I'm one of three women on a shovel in the whole mine. What wears me out is that I'm not even employed by the mine. I'm with a labour hire agency, a company that rents workers to the mine, so I earn less than the person on the next shovel for the same work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you use AI tools every day. Where does that fit in a shovel cab?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: On breaks I ask it about fault codes when the shovel throws one I haven't seen, and it's right most of the time. At night I use it to draft the newsletter for the women-in-mining group and to read the pension rules in plain words, because the agency's letters are written to confuse you. I'm fifty-eight and I talk to a chatbot more than I talk to my supervisor, and honestly the chatbot listens better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame in a way, because the tools are useful. At work I'd tell the crew it's not going to steal their jobs, it's a better manual. Online I'd post that the real fight is still about labour hire and pay, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it changes nothing for me, and that's not entirely good news. I'd still be on agency pay, still with less than a month saved, still hoping my knees last seven more years. The plateau doesn't fix the things that are actually wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and keep teaching the younger operators how to use them on their phones. I'd push the union to make the mine take labour hire workers on as direct employees. And I'd try again to get a bit put aside, but on agency pay that's a wish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit flat, like being told the bus is late again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would the plateau feel flat rather than a relief?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I was half hoping AI might shake things up enough to fix the stupid parts of how we work, like the paperwork that takes an hour every shift. Everyone's scared of the robots. I'm more scared nothing changes and I'm still on agency rates at sixty-four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you end up with so little saved, at your level?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter went to university, first in the family, and I paid what I could. Then the agency cut our site allowance two years ago. Ines works part-time at the library, so we manage, but it's month to month.

S0.say: The tools are useful, so it's a bit of a shame; it's a better manual, not a job thief. The real fight is still about labour hire and pay, not robots.
S0.think: The plateau changes nothing for me, and that's not entirely good news. I'd still be on agency pay with less than a month saved, hoping my knees last seven more years.
S0.do: Keeps using AI tools and teaches younger operators to use them. Pushes the union to have labour hire workers taken on as direct employees, and tries again to save.
S0.feel: Mostly calm, but a little flat, like being told the bus is late again.
S0.quote: Everyone's scared of the robots. I'm more scared nothing changes and I'm still on agency rates at sixty-four.
S0.fieldNote: Elena reverses the usual fear: she worries more about nothing changing than about robots. Her grievance is labour hire pay, which explains her thin savings alongside her daughter's university costs. She is the person on her crew who teaches others to use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance to fix things if we bargain for it. Train everyone, labour hire included, on the new systems, and let the savings pay for it. I'd say that on the union page and at the women-in-mining meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do all right. I learn fast and I'm already using the tools. The danger is that as an agency worker I'm the easiest to drop, however good I am, because they just ring the agency and say don't send her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Within a month I'd apply for any remote operations training, the centre where people run the shovels and trucks from screens in the city. I'd ask the AI to help me write the application and practise the interview. I'd also push the union hard to make sure agency workers get a fair shot at the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, but more excited than scared, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The remote centre is in the city. Would you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines would move tomorrow, she's always wanted to be near the big library. But we couldn't afford city rent on what I earn now, so it would depend on the pay. Maybe I'd do weeks in the city and weeks at home for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joe on the number two shovel. He's brilliant with his hands and terrified of a phone screen. Joe can feel a tooth crack through the joystick, and they'll throw him away because he can't reset a password.

S1.say: This is a chance to fix things if we bargain for it: train everyone, labour hire included, and let the savings pay. She would post it on the union page and at the women-in-mining meeting.
S1.think: I'd probably do all right because I learn fast and already use the tools. But as an agency worker I'm the easiest to drop, however good I am.
S1.do: Applies within a month for remote operations training, using AI to write the application and practise the interview. Pushes the union to give agency workers a fair shot at the course.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, but more excited than scared.
S1.quote: Joe can feel a tooth crack through the joystick, and they'll throw him away because he can't reset a password.
S1.fieldNote: Elena sees steady change as an opening and would move first. Her one real fear is that agency status makes her easy to drop regardless of skill. Her concern for Joe, a gifted operator who struggles with screens, was vivid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that two years is a disgrace if governments don't move. We'd need a basic income or wage guarantee, and the companies that profit should pay for it. I'd organise, march, write, everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, two years beats me too, however quick I am. If AI runs the remote centre, there's no step for me to climb onto. I'd be sixty, an agency worker with no payout coming, because agency workers don't get redundancy from the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the first week, using AI to dig through every rule on what agency workers are owed and what the welfare office would pay us. I'd help organise the labour hire workers into the union properly, because we'd be first out. I'd also try to sell something on the side, maybe teaching older people to use these tools, because there'd be plenty who need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Being quick doesn't help when the floor drops away under everyone at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in those two years that you wouldn't with more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't bother with the remote ops course, because it would be gone before I finished. I'd just put everything into money now and the fight for a safety net. With two years, being an early adopter just means you see the cliff a bit sooner than everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'sell something on the side'. Is that realistic on your shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On my days off, maybe. A few hours a week at the community hall showing people how to talk to the AI about their pension or their bills. It wouldn't replace my pay, but it might pay the power bill.

S2.say: Two years would be a disgrace if governments don't move: there must be a basic income or wage guarantee, paid for by the companies that profit. She would organise, march and write.
S2.think: Two years beats me too, however quick I am, because AI would run the remote centre as well. I'd be sixty, an agency worker with no redundancy from the mine.
S2.do: Uses AI in the first week to find what agency workers are owed and what welfare pays. Organises labour hire workers into the union and starts a small side income teaching older people to use AI.
S2.feel: Alarmed, because being quick doesn't help when the floor drops under everyone at once.
S2.quote: With two years, being an early adopter just means you see the cliff a bit sooner than everyone else.
S2.fieldNote: Even Elena's appetite for change can't beat a two-year timeline, and she said so plainly. Her agency status means no redundancy payout, which sharpens the fear. Her side-income idea uses the same skill that steadies her elsewhere: teaching others to use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do something serious, so let's not waste the first two arguing. Train people, protect pensions, and make the companies pay into a fund. That's what I'd tell anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and I'm sixty-three. I could do the remote ops course and work there for two or three years, maybe as a trainer, then leave. If I get off agency pay along the way, I might even save something for the first time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first six months I'd do the remote operations course and apply to be a direct employee in the centre, not through the agency. I'd use AI to build myself a study plan and to practise the simulator tests. Any pay rise would go straight into savings, not into spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but mostly I feel like I've been given a ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is five years different from two, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a cliff. Five years is a steep hill, and I'm good at hills. Give me five years and I'll teach the robots' minders how a shovel actually feels, and get a pension out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ines say about you starting a new job at fifty-nine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd laugh and say she married a woman who learned to drive a shovel at thirty-five, so why not. Then she'd ask whether we can finally afford a holiday.

S3.say: Five years is enough to do something serious, so let's not waste the first two arguing. Train people, protect pensions and make the companies pay into a fund.
S3.think: Five years puts me at sixty-three, so I could do the remote ops course and work two or three years as a trainer. Getting off agency pay might let me save for the first time.
S3.do: Does the remote operations course in the first six months and applies to join the centre as a direct employee. Uses AI to build a study plan and practise simulator tests, and saves any pay rise.
S3.feel: A little uneasy, but mostly like she's been handed a ladder.
S3.quote: Give me five years and I'll teach the robots' minders how a shovel actually feels, and get a pension out of it.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns the cliff into a hill Elena feels able to climb. The move into remote operations is also her way out of agency pay. Her partner backs her, recalling that Elena learned the shovel at thirty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decade to get it right, so there's no excuse. Every miner should be trained, every pension protected. I'd keep saying it at the union and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is the easy one for me. I'd be sixty-eight, out before it lands. My worry would be my daughter, who works in an office, and the young women I've mentored into the pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep pushing for direct employment. I'd run sessions in the women-in-mining group on using the tools, so the next lot aren't caught short. I'd retire at sixty-five as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for me. Worried for the young ones, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your daughter works in an office. What would you tell her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to learn the tools now, and to save more than I did. I'd tell her what I wish someone had told me at thirty: the job you love is not the same as the job that will love you back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the decade go well for the young miners you've mentored?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid training, on the clock, and a promise that the remote centre hires from the pit first. Not from some city graduate scheme. They know the ore, they should run the machines.

S4.say: Ten years is a decade to get it right, so there's no excuse: train every miner and protect every pension. She would keep saying it at the union and online.
S4.think: Ten years is the easy one for me, because I'd be sixty-eight and out before it lands. My worry is my daughter in her office job and the young women I've mentored.
S4.do: Keeps working and pushing for direct employment, and runs AI sessions for the women-in-mining group. Plans to retire at sixty-five as intended.
S4.feel: Calm for herself, worried for the young ones.
S4.quote: I'd tell her what I wish someone had told me at thirty: the job you love is not the same as the job that will love you back.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade Elena is calm for herself and turns outward to her daughter and her mentees. She wants the remote centre to hire from the pit first. Her advice to her daughter was the most personal line of the interview.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years, no payout because I'm labour hire, nothing saved. What would help is a basic safety net that covers agency workers the same as direct ones, and a pension bridge for people over fifty-five. And training paid for by the companies making the money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about labour hire, and it's the whole story for a lot of us. The robots will take the jobs that are easiest to drop, and the easiest to drop are the agency ones.

headlineQuote: I'm fifty-eight and I talk to a chatbot more than I talk to my supervisor, and honestly the chatbot listens better.
portrait: Elena Lopez is a 58-year-old electric shovel operator and crew lead at an iron ore mine, employed through a labour hire agency on lower pay and with almost nothing saved after helping her daughter through university. She is a progressive, union-minded early adopter who uses AI every day and teaches others to do the same. She worries more about nothing changing than about robots, and sees steady change and five years' warning as a ladder into remote operations. Only the two-year scenario alarms her, because her speed can't help when everyone falls at once.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because as a labour hire worker she would get no payout and has nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: A safety net that covers agency workers the same as direct employees, a pension bridge for over-fifty-fives, and company-paid training.
